title: Pick Your Co-op Role
description: Choose your moves in six chaotic team scenarios, then rank two sets of team habits to see where you lean on the Information–Coordination and Prevention–Recovery scales. No lean is better than another.

sections.title: When Things Go Sideways
sections.description: Six chaotic team moments across games and sports.

sections.title: Your Priorities
sections.description: Two quick rankings.

dimensions.description: Information leans toward learning what is happening first; Coordination leans toward aligning teammates and sharing a plan.
Prevention leans toward blocking trouble before it spreads; Recovery leans toward repairing the situation after something goes wrong.

questions.prompt: In a fictional dungeon game, your squad splits and one teammate is lost. What is your first move?
questions.explanation: Each option is a valid co-op move. This choice shows whether you lean toward gathering information or aligning people, and toward prevention or recovery.

options.label: Guard the exit so everyone has a safe fallback
Scout ahead to check for hazards before anyone moves
Call a meetup point to help the teammate reconnect
Retrace the corridors to find the teammate's last known spot

questions.prompt: In an invented tabletop campaign, a party member is knocked out mid-fight. What do you do?
questions.explanation: There is no better answer here. Your pick reflects whether you reach first for facts or for team alignment, and for stopping further harm or repairing the current one.

options.label: Study the enemy's pattern to learn what it will do next
Organize turns so someone revives the fallen ally
Check the map for which ally is in reach of the revival
Tell everyone to form a tight line and block the enemy

questions.prompt: In an imaginary five-a-side match, the other team suddenly speeds up its passing. How do you respond?
questions.explanation: Both reading the opponent and talking to teammates are useful. This choice shows which one you reach for first, and whether you aim to head off trouble or reset after it.

options.label: Call a quick huddle to reset everyone's positions
Watch who receives the passes to spot the pattern
Shout marking assignments so gaps close before they open
Note which gaps already opened and where the ball goes after

questions.prompt: In a made-up heist game, an alarm starts a countdown and your team scatters. What is your instinct?
questions.explanation: Each response is a normal team tactic. Your choice shows whether you reach for information or alignment, and for stopping problems early or recovering from them.

options.label: Lock the nearest door to slow pursuers before they reach the group
Review the floor plan for the safest route out
Gather the team at one spot and assign who carries what
Check which tools are still missing after the scramble

questions.prompt: Your invented board-game team's shared plan falls apart halfway through. What do you do next?
questions.explanation: Rebuilding a plan and learning why it failed are both reasonable. This choice shows how you lean when a team plan breaks.

options.label: Ask each person for their view, then rebuild one plan together
Quietly investigate what the other side is doing
Assign roles so the same mistake cannot repeat
Work out which step broke and how to patch it

questions.prompt: In a fictional online raid, voice chat cuts out just as the boss changes phase. What do you do?
questions.explanation: No option is ranked above the others. Your pick shows whether you lean toward gathering clues or setting shared signals, and toward guarding or repairing.

options.label: Watch the boss's moves closely and track the new phase
Type short signals so teammates know what to do next
Read the damage log to see who needs help
Take a fixed position so the group's formation holds

questions.prompt: Rank these team jobs from the one you would take first to the one you would take last.
questions.explanation: This ranking is unkeyed. Higher placement for a job shows where your instinct points, and no ordering is better than another.

items.label: Scout the area for what is coming
Secure the route behind the team

questions.prompt: Rank these end-of-round habits from the one you do most naturally to the one you do least.
questions.explanation: This is a preference ranking with no right order. It adds a second view of your leaning between information and coordination, and between prevention and recovery.

items.label: Map the threats for next time
Call a short regroup before the next round
Review what happened to learn from it
Check in with teammates who had a rough round

title: Watch-Party Rulebook
description: Answer four rule-call tasks with explanations, then make four couch-moment choices to reveal your watch-party style on Explainer-Observer and Calm-Loud scales.

sections.title: Rule calls
sections.description: Objective tasks scored for accuracy.

sections.title: Couch moments
sections.description: Taste choices with no right answers.

dimensions.description: Whether you prefer letting the game speak for itself or actively explaining what is happening.
Whether your watch-party energy runs hushed and steady or big and noisy.

questions.prompt: Under FIBA basketball rules, how many points did this team score in total?
questions.context: Tally for one team: 2 made free throws, 3 made shots from inside the three-point line, and 2 made shots from outside it.
questions.explanation: Under FIBA rules a free throw is 1 point, an inside shot 2 and an outside shot 3: 2 + 6 + 6 = 14.

questions.prompt: A newcomer asks why the crowd goes hushed during a goalball rally. Which explanation fits the sport?
questions.explanation: Goalball uses a ball with bells, and players wear eyeshades, so they track play by sound. Spectators stay quiet during play so the bells can be heard.

options.label: Players follow the ball's bells by sound, so spectators stay quiet during play
The referee bans all cheering for the whole match
The ball is silent and the quiet helps referees see it
Quiet is only needed during halftime

questions.prompt: Match each stoppage to the call in the invented Lantern Court rulebook.
questions.context: Invented rules. Offside: an attacker is nearer the goal line than the ball and all defenders but the keeper when a forward pass is played. Net violation: a body touches the net during a rally. Traveling: a carrier takes three steps without bouncing.
questions.explanation: Each play matches one rule definition: the attacker position is offside, touching the net is a net violation, and three unbounced steps is traveling.

left.label: Carrier takes three steps with the ball and no bounce
Striker's hip brushes the net while chasing a ball during a rally
As a forward pass is played, a forward is nearer the goal line than the ball and every defender except the keeper

questions.prompt: Order the invented Lantern Court challenge steps so every stated rule is respected.
questions.context: Invented rules: the clock stops after the flag is raised; review happens after the clock stops; the decision is announced after review; play restarts after the announcement; the scorer updates the sheet after the announcement.
questions.explanation: The flag, clock stop, review and announcement form a chain. Restart and sheet update both follow the announcement, in either order.

questions.prompt: Play stops and a newcomer looks puzzled. What do you do?
questions.explanation: There is no correct answer. This choice shows whether you lean toward explaining or observing, and calm or loud energy.

options.label: Quietly lean over and give a short rule recap
Announce the rule to the whole room with gusto
Stay quiet and let the replay answer it
Cheer and say you will find out together

questions.prompt: During live play, how much rules talk do you want from the room?
questions.explanation: Neither end is better. Your slider position shows how much you favor commentary over letting the game speak.

questions.prompt: Rank these watch-party touches from most to least like you.
questions.explanation: Your ranking has no right answer. Items near the top weigh more toward your style on both scales.

items.label: A printed one-page rule card on the table
A quiet corner for focused watching

questions.prompt: Your team scores. How loud is your ideal reaction?
questions.explanation: Both are valid. This slider shows whether your game-day energy leans hushed or roaring.

title: Soccer Words Across Borders
description: Match everyday football vocabulary across English, Spanish and French, then pick the right term for short invented matchday sentences.

questions.prompt: Match each Spanish football term to its common English meaning.
questions.context: Use everyday matchday meanings. Several terms have regional variants, so this quiz asks for common equivalents only.
questions.explanation: These are commonly used Spanish terms for the playing surface, official, keeper, offside position and corner restart. Regional variants exist, such as arquero for goalkeeper.

questions.prompt: Match each French football term to its common English meaning.
questions.explanation: Terrain commonly means the playing surface, while hors-jeu is the offside term and coup franc a free kick. Gardien de but is the full phrase for goalkeeper.

questions.prompt: In the Spanish sentence “La cancha estaba mojada antes del partido”, which English word fits cancha?
questions.explanation: Cancha names the surface the match is played on, so pitch fits. Field would also be a common English choice, but it is not offered here.

questions.prompt: A French commentator says: “Après le coup de sifflet final, les joueuses ont quitté le terrain.” What does terrain refer to?
questions.explanation: After the final whistle the players leave the surface they were playing on. In football contexts terrain commonly means the playing field, not an event or office.

questions.prompt: In English football talk, which pair of words commonly names the same playing surface?
questions.explanation: Pitch and field are both commonly used for the playing surface, with preference varying by region and speaker. Kit, boot and whistle are equipment.

questions.prompt: Identify the language of each short matchday phrase.
questions.explanation: Accents and word forms give the clues: le and est are French, el and está are Spanish, and the and is are English. Terms cross borders but sentences stay in one language.

questions.prompt: Which Spanish sentence best translates “The referee pointed to the corner flag”?

options.label: El portero señaló el banderín de córner.
El árbitro señaló el banderín de córner.
El árbitro señaló el banco de suplentes.

questions.explanation: Árbitro is the referee and banderín de córner is the corner flag. The other options change the person pointing or the object pointed to.

questions.prompt: A French report says: “L’arbitre a annulé le but pour hors-jeu.” What happened?

options.label: The goal was disallowed for offside.
A free kick was taken near the corner.
The match was moved to another pitch.

questions.explanation: Annuler le but means to cancel the goal, and hors-jeu gives the reason: offside. Nothing in the sentence mentions a substitution, free kick or venue change.

title: Board Game Mechanic Mixer
description: Apply a short original glossary to eight tabletop play moments: pick mechanics, match moments to mechanics, link overlapping ones, and sort mechanics into broader families.

sections.title: Play moments
sections.description: Name the mechanic behind what happens at the table.

sections.title: Mechanic families
sections.description: Group mechanics and spot overlaps.

questions.prompt: You pass cards around the table, keep one, and pass the rest. Which mechanic is this?
questions.context: Glossary: Drafting means choosing one item from a set and passing the remainder on. Set collection means scoring for gathering matching groups. Trick-taking means everyone plays one card per round and one card wins the played cards. Auction means bidding to win an item.
questions.explanation: Keeping one card and passing the rest on is the defining move of drafting. Scoring or winning rounds is a separate matter.

questions.prompt: Match each play moment to the mechanic it shows. Some mechanics are used more than once.
questions.context: Glossary: Drafting: choose one, pass the rest. Set collection: score for matching groups. Worker placement: put a limited token on an action space that blocks others from using it. Area control: earn points for having the most pieces in a region.

left.label: You claim the only market space this round, so nobody else can use it
Three matching tiles earn bonus points; a lone tile earns nothing
You take a card from a fan and hand the rest to your left
Whoever has the most pieces in the northern region scores its points
You gather pairs of the same fruit card to score at game end

questions.explanation: Blocking a space is worker placement, matching groups are set collection, passing the rest is drafting, and majority in a region is area control. Two moments share set collection.

questions.prompt: Each round everyone plays one card face up, and the highest card collects all of them. Which mechanic is this?
questions.context: Glossary: Trick-taking: everyone plays one card per round and one card wins the played cards. Auction: bid to win an item. Set collection: score for matching groups. Drafting: choose one, pass the rest.
questions.explanation: One card per player per round, with a single winner of the pile, is exactly trick-taking. Nothing is bid, passed on, or grouped.

questions.prompt: Choose the mechanic shown in each moment.
questions.context: Glossary: Deck building: add cards to your own deck during play. Auction: bid to win an item. Trick-taking: each player plays one card per round and one wins. Area control: most pieces in a region scores.

cells.label: You start with ten basic cards and buy stronger ones that shuffle into your draw pile
The player who wins the round's played cards leads the next round
Players secretly bid points, and the highest bidder takes the tile

questions.explanation: Growing your own deck is deck building, leading after winning a round is trick-taking, and bidding for a tile is an auction.

questions.prompt: Which pair of mechanics belongs to the same family in this quiz's taxonomy?
questions.context: Taxonomy: Card-play family: the main decision is which cards to choose, pass, or play. Board-space family: the main decision is which locations to occupy. Resource-engine family: the main decision is spending to earn more later.
questions.explanation: Both drafting and trick-taking are about choosing, passing, or playing cards. The other pairs mix a card mechanic with a location or economy mechanic.

questions.prompt: Group each mechanic under its broader family. Several mechanics can share a family.
questions.context: Taxonomy: Card-play: choose, pass, or play cards. Board-space: occupy locations. Resource-engine: spend now to earn more later. Engine building means buying producers that yield more resources each round.
questions.explanation: Trick-taking and drafting center on cards, area control on locations, and engine building on spending for future income. Real games often blend families.

questions.prompt: Link each moment to every mechanic it contains. Moments can show more than one.
questions.context: Glossary: Drafting: choose one, pass the rest. Set collection: score matching groups. Worker placement: place a limited token on an action space that blocks others. Auction: bid to win an item.

left.label: You pick a card, pass the rest, and later score matching pairs
You put a token on an action space that is then closed to others
You bid points for a tile, and same-colored tiles score together

questions.explanation: The first moment combines drafting with set collection, and the third combines an auction with set collection. The blocked action space is worker placement alone.

questions.prompt: Which description contains both trick-taking and drafting?
questions.context: Glossary: Trick-taking: everyone plays one card per round and the winner takes the played cards. Drafting: choose one, pass the rest. Worker placement: place a limited token on a blocking action space. Auction: bid to win an item.

options.label: Everyone plays one card per round and the highest wins the pile
Players pick a card and pass the rest, then play those cards one per round with the highest winning
Players bid for tiles and the highest bid keeps each one
Players place tokens on exclusive action spaces

questions.explanation: Choosing and passing cards is drafting, and playing one card per round for a winner is trick-taking. The other descriptions each show only one mechanic.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: Mechanic names are defined by a short original glossary and taxonomy supplied in each question, not by any rulebook. Real games often blend several mechanics, and families are not universally exclusive. Matches and links earn credit per correct pairing.

title: Sports Equipment Evolution
description: Order invented bats, paddles, balls and helmets using archive clues, then pick the performance or safety reason behind each change.

sections.title: Build the timelines
sections.description: Use the archive clues to order each equipment line.

sections.title: Explain the change
sections.description: Pick the reason that fits the supplied data.

questions.prompt: In the invented sport Netpaddle, order these paddle stages from oldest to newest.
questions.context: Invented club notes: the laminated paddle came after the solid ash paddle. The hollow polymer paddle came after the laminated one. The foam-core carbon paddle came after the hollow polymer one.
questions.explanation: The notes form one chain: solid ash, laminated, hollow polymer, then foam-core carbon. Each clue links to its neighbor.

questions.prompt: In the invented sport Gloveball, order these head-protection stages from oldest to newest.
questions.context: Invented league memos: leather caps came before padded shells. Padded shells came before face-guard shells. The impact liner was offered only on a model that already had a face guard.
questions.explanation: Each memo adds one link: cap, padded shell, face guard, then liner. The liner needed a face-guard model first.

questions.prompt: In the invented sport Tidewick, order these ball stages. Either order is fine where the memos are silent.
questions.context: Invented memos: the bladder-lined leather ball replaced the stitched leather ball. Both the sealed synthetic ball and the textured-grip synthetic ball came after the bladder-lined ball. Nothing says which of those two came first.
questions.explanation: Stitched leather is first and the bladder-lined ball second. The two synthetic balls both follow it, and the memos allow either order between them.

questions.prompt: In the invented sport Bramble, order these bats from oldest to newest using their archive stamps.
questions.context: Invented museum stamps: hickory bat 1899, ash bat 1921, hollow aluminum bat 1974, composite bat 2003.
questions.explanation: Sorting the stamp years gives hickory 1899, ash 1921, aluminum 1974, composite 2003.

questions.prompt: Courtlet racket frames went from wood to carbon fiber. Using the invented guide, which shift raised both power and control?
questions.context: Invented Courtlet guide: a lighter frame allows a faster swing, which this game counts as more power. A frame that bends less under load counts as more control. Test sheet: wood frame 380 g, bends 9 mm under a test load. Carbon frame 300 g, bends 3 mm under the same load.

options.label: Lighter and bends less, so faster swings and more control
Heavier and bends more, so the frame absorbs more of the shot
Lighter and bends more, so the frame springs back harder
Same weight and bend, with only a new paint finish

questions.explanation: The carbon frame is 80 g lighter and bends 6 mm less. Under the guide's stated rules, those two changes mean more power and more control.

questions.prompt: Gloveball added an impact liner under the shell. Why does the test data support this safety change?
questions.context: Invented drop test. Shell only: peak force 160 units lasting 4 ms. Shell with liner: peak force 90 units lasting 9 ms.

options.label: It spreads the impact over more time, lowering the peak force
It stops all contact between the head and the shell
It makes the impact shorter and sharper
It raises the force so players hit more carefully

questions.explanation: The liner stretches the impact from 4 ms to 9 ms, and the peak falls from 160 to 90. It reduces force without removing the impact.

questions.prompt: Tidewick switched to a sealed synthetic ball. What performance reason does the soak test show?
questions.context: Invented soak test, 10 minutes in water. Stitched leather ball gained 90 g. Sealed synthetic ball gained 5 g.

options.label: It absorbs far less water, so weight and handling stay steadier in rain
It absorbs more water, so it grows heavier and slower
It floats higher because it is filled with air
It bounces the same in every test, whatever the conditions

questions.explanation: A 5 g gain against 90 g means the synthetic ball keeps nearly the same weight when wet, so players handle it consistently.

questions.prompt: Which equipment setup lets goalball players follow the ball on equal terms?
questions.context: This uses the real sport of goalball, with details from the cited Paralympic references.

options.label: A ball with bells, with all players wearing eyeshades and the crowd quiet
A silent ball, with eyeshades for only some players
A bell ball with a loud crowd and no eyeshades
A brightly colored ball, so players can track it by sight

questions.explanation: The ball's bells let players track it by sound, eyeshades equalize visual input for everyone, and a quiet crowd keeps the sound audible.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

Paralympic: goalball classification

note: Netpaddle, Gloveball, Tidewick, Bramble and Courtlet are invented sports, and their timelines and test numbers are made up for this quiz. The goalball question uses real published facts.

title: Stadium-City-Country Links
description: Work through invented tournament venue cards, linking each stadium to its host city, then the city to its country, then events to host cities.

questions.prompt: Match each Atlas Cup venue to its host city using the clues.
questions.context: Invented Atlas Cup. Each city hosts one venue. Velmora and Oruvia are coastal; Tavrin and Misqua are inland. Saltwind Arena is coastal but not in Velmora. Lantern Park is coastal. Ridgeback Field's city name starts with M.
questions.explanation: Saltwind must be in Oruvia, leaving Velmora for Lantern Park. Ridgeback takes Misqua, so Copperline Stadium is in Tavrin.

questions.prompt: Which venue hosts the final of the invented Women's Atlas Cup?
questions.context: The final goes to a venue that is the only one in its city and seats over 30,000. Beacon Arena (Kelsa, 28,000); Orchard Stadium (Ponterra, 34,000); Riverbend Park (Kelsa, 31,000); Summit Field (Dunmore, 25,000).
questions.explanation: Ponterra and Dunmore each have one venue. Only Orchard Stadium also seats over 30,000, while Riverbend shares Kelsa with Beacon.

questions.prompt: Which pair of venues shares a country but not a city?
questions.context: Invented cards: Beacon Arena is in Kelsa, Halvern. Orchard Stadium is in Ponterra, Brevland. Riverbend Park is in Kelsa, Halvern. Summit Field is in Dunmore, Brevland.
questions.explanation: Orchard Stadium and Summit Field are both in Brevland but in different cities. Beacon and Riverbend share the city too.

questions.prompt: Link each Atlas Cup city to its country; repeats are allowed.
questions.context: Only Kestria and Daloma host Atlas Cup cities, two each. Oruvia is in Daloma. Velmora is in a different country from Oruvia. Misqua shares a country with Velmora. Tavrin does not share one with Misqua.
questions.explanation: Velmora goes to Kestria, so Misqua does too. Tavrin must join Oruvia in Daloma. Norvane hosts no city here.

questions.prompt: Which fan ticket contains a venue-city-country chain that conflicts with the reference note?
questions.context: Reference: each city is in exactly one country, and Rosmere is in Ilvaria. Tickets: (a) Marlow Park, Quenby, Ilvaria; (b) Gantry Arena, Quenby, Ilvaria; (c) Tidewater Field, Rosmere, Ilvaria; (d) Highmark Stadium, Rosmere, Sundora.
questions.explanation: Rosmere is in Ilvaria, so Highmark Stadium's ticket naming Sundora conflicts. Tickets a, b and c agree with the note.

questions.prompt: Use both tables to find the country for each venue.
questions.context: Invented venue-city table: Cedar Dome in Pell; Mistral Arena in Orrin; Anvil Field in Lisk. City-country table: Orrin in Wyndham; Lisk in Sundora; Pell in Sundora; Dray in Brevland.
questions.explanation: Follow each venue to its city, then that city to its country. Dray is a decoy, and two venues share Sundora.

questions.prompt: Link each invented Atlas Cup match to its host city.
questions.context: Venues: Hollin Dome (Brack, 60,000), Garrow Stadium (Sennet, 41,000), Tern Park (Sennet, 36,000). Men's final: largest venue. Women's final: second largest. Women's semifinal: smallest.
questions.explanation: Sizes give Hollin, Garrow and Tern in that order. Both women's matches therefore land in Sennet, while Dovre hosts nothing.

questions.prompt: Which statement must be true given this invented link map?
questions.context: Lumen Arena and Fern Park are in Dovre. Quarry Field is in Mirel. Pier Stadium is in Vesk. Dovre and Mirel are in Karsa. Vesk is in Orlen.
questions.explanation: Dovre and Mirel are both in Karsa, so Lumen Arena and Quarry Field share a country. Their cities differ, and Pier Stadium is in Orlen.

options.label: Fern Park and Pier Stadium share a country
Lumen Arena and Quarry Field share a country
Quarry Field and Pier Stadium share a city
Lumen Arena and Quarry Field share a city

questions.prompt: Using the minute stamps in this invented women's football recap, arrange the four moments from earliest to latest.
questions.context: Invented recap, Harbor City v Lakeside, dated 18 Oct 2026. Minute stamps come from the match clock.

items.label: Red card shown to Lakeside defender, 58'

questions.explanation: Sorting by match clock gives 12', 34', 58', then 81'. Stamps, not storylines, decide the order.

questions.prompt: Arrange these four moments from an invented men's handball semi-final by elapsed minute, earliest first.
questions.context: Invented recap, Red Pines v Cedars, dated 18 Oct 2026. Stamps are elapsed minutes of play.

items.label: Cedars late goal that ties the match, 52'

questions.prompt: This invented field hockey recap gives clues instead of times. Arrange the four moments so every clue holds.
questions.context: Invented recap, women's match. The opening goal came before the goalkeeper change. The goalkeeper change came before the green card. The green card came before the late winner.
questions.explanation: The three clues form one chain: opening goal, goalkeeper change, green card, late winner. No other arrangement satisfies all three.

questions.prompt: Using the score after each event, which goal first put the eventual winner ahead?
questions.context: Invented men's football match, score shown as Ridgemont–Calder. Start 0–0. After 9' goal: 1–0. After 27' goal: 1–1. After 44' goal: 2–1. After 61' goal: 2–2. After 70' goal: 2–3. No more goals; 70' goal is the last.
questions.explanation: Calder won 3–2 but never led until the 70' goal made it 2–3. The 27' and 61' goals only tied the match.

questions.prompt: Which numbered event produced the last change of lead in this invented women's basketball finish?
questions.context: FIBA-style scoring: free throw 1, basket inside the arc 2, basket outside the arc 3. Score Aurora–Tide starts 48–48. Events: 1) Tide scores inside the arc. 2) Aurora scores outside the arc. 3) Tide scores outside the arc. 4) Aurora makes one free throw. Event 4 ends the game.
questions.explanation: Scores run 48–50, 51–50, 51–53, 52–53. Tide regained the lead at event 3 and kept it, since event 4 left Aurora one point behind.

questions.prompt: Classify what each score change did, using only the before and after scores.
questions.context: Invented volleyball-style rally scores, shown as Comets–Falcons. Each cell is one point scored by whichever team's number rose.
questions.explanation: Compare who led before and after. Only 1–1 to 1–2 creates a new lead; 3–1 to 3–2 shrinks a gap; 2–3 to 3–3 ties; 4–2 to 5–2 widens a lead.

questions.prompt: Which statement does this invented official match record actually establish?
questions.context: Invented record, Summit v Delta men's basketball final, dated 18 Oct 2026. Final score: Summit 71, Delta 68. Lead changes: 5. Ties: 3. Delta led 66–64 with two minutes left. The record lists no coaching instructions and no player comments.

options.label: A tactical timeout changed how Summit played
Delta lost confidence late in the game

questions.explanation: Only the 71–68 final score is recorded. Tactics, confidence and causes are interpretations, and the record lists nothing that supports them.

questions.prompt: Three sources give different times for the same invented goal. Under the stated league rule, which should anchor the timeline?
questions.context: Invented league rule: the official match report signed by the match officials is the record of truth for all timestamps. Sources for one goal: a morning recap says 74'. An unofficial fan clip log says 75'. The official match report says 76'.
questions.explanation: The league rule names the signed official report as the record of truth, so 76' anchors the timeline. Averaging would create a time that no record of truth gives.

title: The Court Is a Diagram
description: Read court outlines, tap labeled zones and match markings to rules in eight short diagram puzzles, scored for accuracy.

questions.prompt: Which invented sport matches a diagram with a center line, two restricted areas and no net?
questions.context: Invented guide. Net Nine: center net, no restricted areas. Zone Toss: center line, two restricted areas, no net. Arc Ball: center line, two arcs, no restricted areas. Pole Run: no center line, one restricted area.
questions.explanation: Only Zone Toss has a center line, two restricted areas and no net. Each other sport differs on at least one of those features.

questions.prompt: How far is each restricted area's inner edge from the center line?
questions.context: Invented Pole Run field: 40 units long with a center line at the midpoint. Each end has a restricted area 6 units deep, measured inward from the end line.
questions.explanation: The center line is 20 units from each end. Subtracting the 6-unit restricted area leaves 14 units between its inner edge and the center line.

questions.prompt: Attackers throw left to right. Tap the zone attackers may never enter.
questions.context: Invented Zone Toss rules: attackers start every point in the left back corner and must cross the center line. The left restricted area is open to all players. Only defenders may stand in the restricted area on the right.
questions.explanation: The right restricted area is reserved for defenders. The left restricted area is open to everyone, the left corner is the attackers' start spot, and attackers must cross the center line.

title: Name the Game by Its Rules
description: Connect invented game clues to every genre label that fits the supplied definitions, then pick the feature that separates two overlapping genres.

sections.title: Tag the play
sections.description: Link each clue to all genres it supports.

sections.title: Spot the difference
sections.description: Find the feature that separates two genres.

questions.prompt: Connect each play clue to every genre label it supports under the definitions given.
questions.context: Real-time strategy (RTS): all players act continuously without turns, gathering resources and training units. 4X: empire-scale play built on exploring, expanding, exploiting resources and defeating rivals, turn-based or real-time. Tower defense: you place stationary defenders to stop enemy waves on a fixed route.
questions.explanation: The first clue runs in continuous time with gathering and training, so it fits RTS. It also explores, expands, exploits resources and aims to defeat rivals, so it fits 4X. Stationary cannons on a fixed road are tower defense. Turn-taking conquest is 4X but not RTS.

left.label: You scout fogged land, found towns, gather wood, train archers and aim to defeat rival empires while all players act in continuous time.
You place stationary cannons beside a road while invader waves walk the fixed route.
You take turns moving scouts, founding cities and harvesting resources until one empire conquers the rest.

questions.prompt: Connect each play clue to every genre label it supports under these definitions.
questions.context: Roguelike: every run is freshly generated and defeat ends that run's progress. Deckbuilder: cards you add or upgrade form the deck that determines your actions. Platformer: core play is moving and jumping between platforms and hazards. Metroidvania: one connected world where new abilities unlock areas previously blocked.
questions.explanation: A new world each attempt with a restart is roguelike. The castle clue combines jumping with an ability opening an earlier blocked door. Card rewards plus generated-map defeat fit deckbuilder and roguelike.

left.label: Each attempt starts in freshly generated rooms, and when your hero falls you restart at the entrance.
You jump spikes onto moving ledges, then a double-jump reaches a sealed door earlier in the same castle map.
After each fight you pick a card for your deck; a defeat sends you back to a freshly generated map.

questions.prompt: Connect each clue to every genre label it supports under the supplied definitions.
questions.context: Battle royale: many players fight on a shrinking area until one player or squad remains. Hero shooter: players pick named characters with distinct abilities in a shooting game. MOBA: two teams, one character per player, pushing lanes to destroy the enemy base.
questions.explanation: The lane-pushing teams are MOBA. The island with a shrinking zone is battle royale. The last clue adds named characters with unique abilities and first-person shooting, so it fits both battle royale and hero shooter.

left.label: Ten players form two teams, each controlling one champion, and push three lanes toward the enemy base.
Forty players drop onto an island whose safe zone shrinks; the last squad alive wins.
Sixty players choose named characters with unique ultimate abilities, shoot in first person, and the last squad standing wins as the zone shrinks.

questions.prompt: Connect each play description to every label it supports: city builder, survival, sandbox or crafting.
questions.context: City builder: you plan roads, zones and services for a growing settlement. Survival: you manage resources to stay alive against environmental threats. Sandbox: open-ended play with no fixed win condition. Crafting: you combine gathered items into new tools or structures.
questions.explanation: The town planner is a city builder with no final goal, so also sandbox. The rescue-boat clue is survival and crafting but has a fixed goal. The block-builder is sandbox and crafting without any fail state.

left.label: You zone neighborhoods, lay bus routes and watch tax income as the town grows, with no final goal.
You gather wood and stone, combine them into axes and walls, and keep a fire lit through freezing nights until a rescue boat arrives.
You place blocks and combine ores into new tools to build whatever you like; there is no objective or fail state.

questions.prompt: Both real-time strategy and turn-based strategy let you build bases and command armies. Which feature distinguishes real-time strategy?
questions.context: Turn-based strategy: players act in alternating turns. Either genre may include resource gathering, terrain and unit production.
questions.explanation: Gathering, terrain and army command appear in both genres. What defines real-time strategy is that everyone acts at once on a running clock instead of waiting for a turn.

options.label: Players gather resources to pay for units
Players act simultaneously with no waiting for turns
The map contains different terrain types

questions.prompt: Which feature distinguishes a roguelite from a strict roguelike under these definitions?
questions.context: Strict roguelike: each run is freshly generated and defeat ends all progress. Roguelite: runs are also freshly generated, but some earnings persist afterward.
questions.explanation: Generated levels and run-ending defeat are shared by both. A roguelite keeps something, such as currency for permanent upgrades, between runs; a strict roguelike does not.

options.label: Levels are generated anew each run

questions.prompt: A 4X game and a city builder both involve placing buildings. Which feature distinguishes the 4X game?
questions.context: City builder: planning a settlement's growth, possibly with no opponents. 4X: exploring, expanding, exploiting resources and defeating rival factions.
questions.explanation: Building, collecting income and watching growth all occur in city builders. Competing with or eliminating rival factions is built into the 4X definition.

options.label: Competing with or eliminating rival factions is core play
Players collect taxes or other income
Players place structures on a map

questions.prompt: A visual novel and an adventure game both tell stories. Which feature distinguishes the adventure game?
questions.context: Visual novel: story told mainly through text and art with occasional choices. Adventure game: story advances by exploring places, collecting items and solving puzzles. Both can branch.
questions.explanation: Stories, characters and branching can appear in both. The adventure game is set apart by item collection and puzzle solving as the way the story moves forward.

options.label: It can branch into different endings
It presents story through text and art
Progress depends on collecting items and solving puzzles

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All game clues are invented, and each question supplies the genre definitions it uses. Real games blur these genres, so treat the definitions as this quiz's rubric rather than a universal taxonomy.

title: The Scorekeeper's Dictionary
description: Connect scoring terms to invented sports from short rule cards, compare words that change meaning between games, then decide whether play scores or continues.

questions.prompt: Connect each scoring term to every invented sport whose rule card uses that term.
questions.context: Invented games. Tidepool Toss: a match has 6 frames, and each frame gives both teams 3 throws. Lantern Ladder: a match has 4 innings, and points are counted in one frame per inning. Court Kite: every rally ends in an immediate point for one side.
questions.explanation: Frames appear in both Tidepool Toss and Lantern Ladder, innings only in Lantern Ladder. Court Kite awards a point on every rally, which is rally-point scoring.

questions.prompt: Connect each term to every invented sport that uses it in the rule cards.
questions.context: Invented games. Pebble Pins: best of three sets; if sets are tied 1-1, a tiebreak decides the match. Marsh Puck: four periods of 10 minutes; if tied afterward, a shootout tiebreak decides it. Ember Net: two periods of 12 minutes, and ties stay ties.
questions.explanation: Set belongs only to Pebble Pins. Period is used by Marsh Puck and Ember Net. Tiebreaks exist in Pebble Pins and Marsh Puck, but Ember Net allows ties.

questions.prompt: Match each scoring term to the invented sport that owns it. Sports may be used more than once.
questions.context: Invented games. Dune Darts: first to win 3 legs; a leg ends when a player reaches exactly zero, called a checkout. Brook Skittles: 10 frames; a spare closes a frame by clearing all pins in two rolls. Reed Court: each rally gives one point immediately.
questions.explanation: Leg and checkout are both Dune Darts terms, while spare and frame belong to Brook Skittles. Rally point matches Reed Court's immediate point on every rally.

questions.prompt: Both games are at 6-4 in a set. Which statement is correct?
questions.context: Invented rules. In Pebble Pins, a set ends at 6 points if the leader is ahead by 2. In Reed Court, a set ends at 11 points, with no minimum lead.
questions.explanation: The same word has different targets. Pebble Pins has reached 6 with a 2-point lead, so the set ends, while Reed Court is still far from 11.

options.label: Pebble Pins ends; Reed Court continues
Reed Court ends; Pebble Pins continues

questions.prompt: A player completes 4 frames in each game. What is the maximum number of rolls and throws combined?
questions.context: Invented rules. A Brook Skittles frame allows at most 2 rolls. A Tidepool Toss frame gives each player 3 throws.
questions.explanation: Brook Skittles allows 4 × 2 = 8 rolls. Tidepool Toss allows 4 × 3 = 12 throws. Together that is 20, because the word frame has two meanings here.

questions.prompt: For each Court Kite situation, decide who scores or whether play continues.
questions.context: Invented rules. A rally ends when the kite lands on a floor or a team faults. A kite landing inside a side's court scores for the other side. Clipping the net but crossing is legal. A side may touch the kite 3 times in a row; a fourth touch is a fault, and a fault gives the point to the other side. A kite landing outside the lines scores for the side that did not last strike it.
questions.explanation: A legal net clip that lands in Side B's court scores for Side A. B's fourth touch is a fault, so A scores. An out ball goes against the last striker. A second touch is allowed, so that rally continues.

cells.label: Side A's strike clips the net and lands inside Side B's court.
Side B touches the kite four times in a row before it crosses.
Side A strikes the kite and it lands outside the sideline untouched.
Side B returns the kite on its second touch and it is still airborne over the net.

questions.prompt: Under FIBA scoring, a player makes two free throws, one basket inside the three-point line and one beyond it. Total points?
questions.context: Use FIBA official basketball rules scoring, not another league's rulebook.
questions.explanation: Under FIBA scoring, each free throw is worth 1 point, a basket inside the three-point line 2, and one beyond it 3. That gives 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 7.

questions.prompt: After four innings, what happens in this Lantern Ladder game?
questions.context: Invented rules. A tied game after four innings adds one extra inning, and draws are not allowed. Inning scores: Side A 2, 0, 3, 1. Side B 1, 2, 0, 3.
questions.explanation: Side A totals 2 + 0 + 3 + 1 = 6, and Side B totals 1 + 2 + 0 + 3 = 6. The tie means play continues with an extra inning.

options.label: The game ends in a draw

note: Most sports, rule cards and scores here are invented for this quiz and supplied in each question, so you can answer from the cards alone. Only the basketball question uses real FIBA scoring; other leagues may differ.

title: Boss Fight Logic Grid
description: Solve three hero-and-boss assignment grids, run three deduction checks, then repair two broken battle plans. Every grid has exactly one solution; the ordering task accepts any order that obeys its rules.

sections.title: Encounter Grids
sections.description: Assign each hero to a boss using the clues.

sections.title: Deduction Checks
sections.description: Short reasoning tasks about turns, order and elimination.

sections.title: Repair Round
sections.description: Fix plans that break the rules.

questions.prompt: Match each hero to the boss they will fight. Each boss is fought by exactly one hero.
questions.context: Heroes: Mira (healer), Joss (archer), Tane (knight). Bosses: Cinder Golem (fire), Gale Wyvern (flyer), Moss Troll (earth). Clues: the healer will not face fire. The archer faces the flyer.
questions.explanation: The archer Joss takes the flyer. The healer cannot take fire, so Mira faces the Troll. That leaves the Cinder Golem for Tane.

questions.prompt: Four heroes, four bosses, one fight each. Fill in every pairing using the clues.
questions.context: Heroes: Ana (mage), Bo (rogue), Cai (healer), Dev (tank). Bosses: Frost Giant, Storm Hawk (flyer), Lava Slug (fire), Shade (ghost). Clues: the tank faces a fire boss. The mage faces neither the ghost nor the flyer. The healer does not face the flyer.
questions.explanation: Dev takes the fire boss. Ana can only take the Frost Giant. Cai avoids the Hawk and the Giant is gone, so Cai faces the Shade. Bo gets the Hawk.

questions.prompt: Solve the final grid: pair each hero with a boss so every clue holds.
questions.context: Heroes: Rin, Sol, Teo, Uma. Bosses: Bog Hydra (lives in the bog), Sky Titan (lives in the sky), Ice Wraith, Iron Colossus. Clues: Rin faces neither the Hydra nor the Titan. Sol does not face the Wraith. Sol's boss lives neither in the bog nor in the sky. Teo faces the Titan or the Wraith. Uma faces neither the Titan nor the Colossus.
questions.explanation: Sol avoids Wraith, bog and sky, so Sol faces the Colossus. Rin then must take the Wraith. Teo is left with the Titan, and Uma gets the Hydra.

questions.prompt: On which turn does the boss first reach 0 HP or below?
questions.context: The boss starts with 50 HP. Each turn the mage deals 14 and the archer deals 9. After each turn, if the boss is still alive, it heals 5 HP.
questions.explanation: Each full round deals 23. After turn 1: 27, heals to 32. After turn 2: 9, heals to 14. On turn 3 the 23 damage drops it below 0.

questions.prompt: Put the raid opening in an order that obeys every rule.
questions.context: Rules: the barrier must be raised before the tank taunts. The tank must taunt before the mage fires. The archer must mark the weak point before the mage fires. The rogue loots only after the mage has fired.
questions.explanation: Barrier precedes taunt, taunt precedes fire, mark precedes fire, and looting comes after fire. The mark can slot anywhere before the mage fires, so several orders work.

questions.prompt: Which hero faces the Raven?
questions.context: Heroes: Kei, Lia, Max. Bosses: Ogre, Pixie, Raven (the only flyer). Clues: Lia does not face the flyer. Lia does not face the Pixie. Max faces the Ogre or the Pixie. Kei does not face the Ogre.
questions.explanation: Lia avoids the Raven and Pixie, so she faces the Ogre. Max must then face the Pixie. That leaves the Raven for Kei.

questions.prompt: Exactly one swap of two heroes' bosses makes this plan satisfy every rule. Which swap?
questions.context: Rules: the healer does not face fire. The archer faces the flyer. The tank faces a ground boss. The mage does not face a ground boss. Ground bosses: Magma Beast (fire) and Stone Ogre. Cloud Serpent flies. Crypt Lich is neither. Current plan: Healer–Magma Beast, Tank–Stone Ogre, Archer–Cloud Serpent, Mage–Crypt Lich.
questions.explanation: Only the healer breaks a rule, facing fire. Swapping healer and tank sends the healer to the Ogre and the tank to the Magma Beast, which is still ground. Other swaps break the archer or mage rule.

questions.prompt: The old plan failed. Build the repaired plan that satisfies all the new rules.
questions.context: Heroes: Zed, Yara, Wen. Bosses: Ice Lord, Fire Wyrm, Wind Roc. Old plan: Zed–Ice Lord, Yara–Fire Wyrm, Wen–Wind Roc. New rules: Wen cannot face wind. Yara cannot face fire. Zed faces fire or wind. Only Yara has a wind-proof cloak, so Yara faces the wind boss.
questions.explanation: Yara takes the Wind Roc. Zed must then take fire, since wind is gone. That leaves the Ice Lord for Wen, who is allowed to face ice.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All heroes, bosses and rules are invented for these puzzles, and every clue you need is given in the puzzle. Roles and bosses are labeled with text, so no colors are needed.

title: What Survives the Reload?
description: Read the save rules of invented puzzle games, work out what returns after a reload, then arrange steps so your progress survives.

sections.title: Read the Event Log
sections.description: Pick the state restored after a reload.

sections.title: Plan the Sequence
sections.description: Order steps so the goal survives.

questions.prompt: After the reload at step 6, which inventory does the player have?
questions.context: Invented game Lantern Trail: touching a checkpoint stores your current inventory. Reloading restores the last checkpoint touched; items found later are lost. Log: 1) Pick up map. 2) Touch checkpoint A. 3) Pick up rope. 4) Touch checkpoint B. 5) Find brass key. 6) Fall into pit and reload.
questions.explanation: Checkpoint B was the last one touched, and it stored the map and rope. The brass key was found afterward, so it is not restored.

questions.prompt: After the crash, what are the coin count and door state on reload?
questions.context: Invented game Orbit Garage: entering a level makes an autosave; the player can also save manually. Reload loads whichever save is most recent. Log: Enter level 2 with 10 coins (autosave). Collect 5 coins. Save manually. Collect 8 coins. Unlock the vault door. Crash and reload.
questions.explanation: The manual save is the most recent save, made at 15 coins before the door was unlocked. The later 8 coins and the unlocked door are not stored.

questions.prompt: After losing all lives and reloading, what are the gem count and character status?
questions.context: Invented game Starlit Run: gems roll back to the last checkpoint on reload. Unlocking a character writes to a permanent profile immediately and is never rolled back. Log: Touch checkpoint with 3 gems. Collect 4 gems. Unlock the character Mira. Lose all lives and reload.
questions.explanation: Gems return to the checkpoint total of 3. The character unlock lives in the permanent profile, so Mira stays unlocked.

questions.prompt: After the reload, where does the player start and what do they carry?
questions.context: Invented game Cliffside Courier has one save slot and checkpoints on a route in order A, B, C, D. Touching a checkpoint overwrites the slot only if it lies further along the route than the saved one. Log: Hold torch, touch A. Pick up compass, touch C. Walk back and touch B. Pick up shield. Fall and reload.
questions.explanation: Checkpoint B is earlier on the route than C, so it does not overwrite the save. Reload returns to C with the torch and compass, without the shield.

options.label: Checkpoint B with torch, compass and shield
Checkpoint C with torch and compass
Checkpoint C with torch, compass and shield

questions.prompt: Arrange the steps so the lamp and key both survive the rockfall reload and can open the gate.
questions.context: Invented game Ravine Keep: touching a checkpoint stores your inventory, and a rockfall forces a reload to the last checkpoint. The vault gate needs the key and is used after the reload. Steps not constrained by these rules may go in any order.
questions.explanation: Both items must be collected before the checkpoint stores them, and the checkpoint must precede the rockfall. The gate is used after reloading. Lamp and key may swap places.

items.label: Open the vault gate with the key

questions.prompt: Arrange the steps so a defeat in the boss fight reloads you with the bridge down and shield equipped.
questions.context: Invented game Tide Temple: saving at a statue stores switch states and equipped gear, not carried gear. A shield must be taken from its chest before it can be equipped. The boss fight ends in defeat and a reload to the last statue save.
questions.explanation: The chest must be opened before the shield is equipped, and the equip and the bridge switch must both happen before the statue save. Defeat comes last. The switch may come earlier or later than the chest steps.

questions.prompt: Arrange the steps so that after the pit reload the amber token is held and the gate is still open.
questions.context: Invented game Garden Gates: a post save stores inventory and gate states. The spring gate closes permanently once crossed, and the pit sits beyond the gate. The reload goes to the last post save.
questions.explanation: The token must be taken before saving, and the save must happen before crossing, or it would store a closed gate. The pit fall comes after crossing, so the order is fully fixed.

items.label: Fall into the pit and reload

questions.prompt: Arrange the steps so that after the crash you keep the 50 banked points and the key.
questions.context: Invented game Rally Vault: the bank terminal permanently stores score earned so far, while unbanked score is lost on reload. Checkpoints store the key. Winning Race 1 earns 50 points. The crash forces a reload to the last checkpoint.
questions.explanation: The race must be won before banking, and the key must be held before the checkpoint stores it. Both the bank and the checkpoint must happen before the crash. The two chains can interleave.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All games, save rules and event logs here are invented for this quiz. They say nothing about how any real game saves progress.

title: Table Rules Lawyer
description: Read invented tabletop rule cards, apply their stated priority rules to rule on disputes, then spot when the rulebook is missing a rule needed for a unique ruling.

sections.title: Disputes
sections.description: Apply the printed priority rules to the cards in play.

sections.title: Clarification
sections.description: Decide when the rulebook is not enough.

questions.prompt: Mara has 10 life and is shielded. Cinder Strike hits her. What is her life afterward?
questions.context: Invented game Lanternfall. Ward card: "While shielded, ignore all damage." Cinder Strike card: "Deal 3 damage." Priority rule: an effect that ignores damage beats an effect that deals damage, unless the ignoring card names an exception. Ward names none.
questions.explanation: The priority rule lets Ward's ignore effect beat Cinder Strike's deal effect, and Ward lists no exception. Mara takes no damage and stays at 10 life.

questions.prompt: Put these four effects in the order they resolve this round.
questions.context: Lanternfall resolution rule: effects resolve by their printed type, in this fixed sequence: Prevent first, then Deal, then Heal, then Cleanup last.
questions.explanation: The type sequence is fixed: Frost Veil (Prevent), Cinder Bolt (Deal), Fern Salve (Heal), then Lantern Tidy (Cleanup).

questions.prompt: For each character, can they move this turn?
questions.context: Sprint card: "Any character may move 2 spaces." Mud card: "Characters in a swamp cannot move." Boots card: "The wearer ignores Mud." Rules: a narrower card beats a broader one, and an ignore effect beats a cannot effect.
questions.explanation: Mud is narrower than Sprint, so the swamp walker is stuck. The road walker is untouched by Mud. Boots ignore Mud, so Sprint applies again.

cells.label: Ines stands in a swamp with no boots
Wen stands in a swamp wearing Boots

questions.prompt: Dara plays Windfall as her first draw this turn. How many cards does she draw?
questions.context: Windfall card: "Draw 2 cards." Hand Rule card: "No player may draw more than 1 card per turn." Priority rule: a limit reduces an amount down to the limit but does not cancel the action.
questions.explanation: The limit does not cancel Windfall. It only caps the amount, so Dara draws up to the limit of 1 card.

questions.prompt: Match each dispute to the named rule that settles it.
questions.context: R1 Ignore-First: ignore or prevent effects beat deal effects. R2 Narrower-Wins: a card naming a narrower group beats one naming a wider group. R3 Cap: a limit lowers an amount to the limit without cancelling it.
questions.explanation: The cloak ignores damage (R1). The crypt is a narrower group than all heroes (R2). Coin purse and draw limit are both caps on amounts (R3).

left.label: Raiders deal 5 damage, but a Cloak ignores damage
All heroes may rest anywhere, but heroes in the Crypt may not rest
Gain 6 coins, but a purse holds at most 4
Draw 3 cards, but at most 2 may be drawn per turn

questions.prompt: In round 2, an archer attacks a hidden enemy unit while both Fog and Volley are in effect. What does the rulebook force?
questions.context: Fog card, played round 1 and still in effect: "Attacks against hidden units miss." Volley card, played round 2: "Attacks by archers always hit." The only priority rule is Narrower-Wins, and neither group (attacks on hidden units, attacks by archers) is narrower than the other.
questions.explanation: Both cards apply to this attack. Narrower-Wins cannot separate them, and no other rule orders them, so the rulebook gives no unique ruling.

options.label: No unique ruling: the rules give no priority here
Both cards cancel and the attack is rerolled

questions.prompt: For each dispute, is there a unique ruling or insufficient information?
questions.context: Complete priority list: (1) a cannot effect beats a may effect; (2) an ignore effect beats a deal effect. No other priorities exist.
questions.explanation: Rule 1 settles the draw dispute. The discard-versus-keep conflict has no matching rule. In the third case the shield isn't active, so the ignore effect never applies and the attack deals 3.

cells.label: "You may draw 2" versus "No one can draw this turn"
"Players must discard 2" versus "Players must keep 3 cards"
"Attacks deal 3" versus "Ignore damage while shielded," and the target is not shielded

questions.prompt: Which single added rule gives the Fog and Volley dispute a unique ruling?
questions.context: Same dispute: Fog (round 1) says attacks against hidden units miss. Volley (round 2) says archer attacks always hit. Neither group is narrower.
questions.explanation: Cards played later win ties, and Volley was played in round 2, so it beats Fog. The other options leave the hit-or-miss conflict untouched.

options.label: When two cards tie in narrowness, the later-played card wins
Archers roll two dice when attacking
Hidden units start the game with 3 life
Each round lasts exactly four turns

note: Lanternfall and every card, rule and priority list here are invented for this quiz and do not come from any real tabletop game. Each puzzle supplies all the rules you need.

title: Adaptive Sports Rules Primer
description: Eight tasks on how goalball and invented adaptive games use equipment and rules to keep competition fair, from matching adaptations to purposes to making rulings.

questions.prompt: In goalball, what role does sound play, and why do players wear eyeshades?
questions.explanation: The ball contains bells so players track it by sound, and eyeshades give every player the same visual input.

options.label: Bells let players locate the ball by sound; eyeshades equalize visual input
Bells tell referees about fouls; eyeshades protect eyes from the ball
Bells keep the match time; eyeshades hide the ball's color
Bells entertain the crowd; eyeshades are optional for some players

questions.prompt: What should spectators do while the ball is in play at a goalball match?
questions.explanation: Players rely on hearing the bells, so the crowd stays quiet during play and can celebrate when play stops.

options.label: Cheer constantly to support the players
Stay quiet during play so the ball can be heard
Clap in rhythm to guide the ball
Call out directions to the defenders

questions.prompt: A goalball team includes players with different amounts of vision. Which eyeshade rule applies?
questions.explanation: Every player wears eyeshades, which keeps the visual conditions the same for everyone on court.

options.label: Only players with some vision wear eyeshades
Eyeshades are worn only in the second half

questions.prompt: Match each adaptation from these invented games to the purpose it serves.
questions.context: Echo Hockey, Tunnel Tag and Pool Relay are invented games used for practice. Each adaptation below belongs to one of them.
questions.explanation: Sound cues let players find the ball, touch markings show position, and universal eyeshades equalize vision. Quiet rules protect the sound cues.

left.label: Echo Hockey ball filled with bells
Echo Hockey court lines raised with tape
Eyeshades for every Echo Hockey player
Quiet crowd while the Echo Hockey ball moves
Eyeshades for every Tunnel Tag player
Textured rope lane dividers in Pool Relay
