description: Work through invented museum and community record packets about made-up ballgames, then pick the careful, well-sourced way to describe where each game came from.

sections.title: Reading the records
sections.description: Match, judge and sequence evidence.

sections.title: Choosing context
sections.description: Pick careful wording for displays.

questions.prompt: Match each invented game to what its supplied records show about its origin.
questions.context: Invented records. Ringfall: a lab-dated court stone and a community oral history agree on place and period. Stickcatch: two community archives name different valleys as first home, with no physical evidence. Batline: the only item is a printed rulebook from year 1905. Cordtoss: two separate ledgers and a carved board all point to the same fair and period. Hoopwall: a museum label credits one coach, but that coach's diary says the game was adapted from an older village game.

right.label: Origin not shown by the records supplied

questions.explanation: Independent records that agree support an origin. Conflicting claims make it debated. A single modern rulebook shows only when rules were printed, not where the game began.

questions.prompt: Judge each claim about Ringfall against the record. Which claims go beyond what is documented?
questions.context: Invented Ringfall record: a museum holds court stones dated by a lab to year 40 of the Reed Era. The Tessa Valley Council's oral history says the game was played at harvest time. No record names an inventor or lists other places where it was played.

cells.label: Ringfall was played at harvest time.
The court stones date to year 40.
Ringfall was never played outside Tessa Valley.

questions.explanation: Absence of a record is not proof of absence. The packet cannot show an inventor or rule out other places, so those claims overreach.

questions.prompt: Put these four Cordtoss evidence events in order from earliest to latest.
questions.context: Invented dates in Reed Era years: the carved board was made in year 210. The first Marsh Fair ledger entry is year 230. The printed rulebook is year 260. The museum acquired the board in year 905.
questions.explanation: Sorting by the supplied years gives 210, 230, 260, then 905. Later museum records can describe an object but do not make the game itself newer.

questions.prompt: An invented museum label says Odessa Marlow invented Reedline in year 100, citing nothing. An invented community archive says Reedline is older. What is the careful summary?

options.label: Marlow invented Reedline, since a museum said so
The origin is debated, and the label gives no cited support
The community archive is automatically correct
The origin is settled because both sources exist

questions.explanation: Two conflicting claims, one uncited, mean the origin is debated. A careful summary reports both and notes which has supporting evidence, without declaring a winner.

questions.prompt: An exhibit about Cordtoss needs a community name. Which wording follows the consent record?
questions.context: Invented consent note: the community's own archive and signed form ask to be named the Reedmarsh Collective. Older pamphlets used the label 'Marsh Fair people', which the collective did not choose.
questions.explanation: Communities should be named as they ask to be named. The signed consent record outranks older outside labels.

questions.prompt: The word 'kora' means different games in two valleys. Which label for a Westmere hand-strike ball is least ambiguous?
questions.context: Invented language note: in Eastgate speech, 'kora' means a kicked-ball game. In Westmere speech, 'kora' means a hand-strike ballgame. The museum ball came from Westmere.
questions.explanation: Naming the specific game and valley removes the ambiguity. A bare word can point to different games, and 'ancestor of all' is an unsupported claim.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Batline fits the Port Alder records without overreaching?
questions.context: Invented records: the Port Alder Batline Club printed its modern rules in year 1905. Separate village ledgers from year 1700 describe stick-and-ball games with different rules and no shared name.

options.label: Port Alder invented every stick-and-ball game
Modern rules were printed in 1905; older stick-and-ball games had other rules

questions.explanation: The records separate two things: the 1905 rule publication and earlier related games. Mixing them would credit the club with the whole history.

questions.prompt: Under the packet's curation policy, what must happen before the Hollow Creek ball story card goes on display?
questions.context: Invented policy: story cards about community objects are shown only after the community's knowledge-holders consent and review the wording. Public availability of a record does not count as consent.

options.label: Borrow a similar story from a neighboring town
Hollow Creek knowledge-holders consent and review the wording
Use the catalog entry because it is public
Shorten it to a single-origin claim

questions.explanation: The policy requires consent and review from the community itself. Public records, borrowed stories or simplified origin claims do not replace that.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All games, communities, museums, dates and records in this quiz are invented for practice in reading evidence. They do not describe real Indigenous or other traditions, and the answers rely only on the records supplied in each question.

title: What Is That Game Sound Telling You?
description: Learn a small legend of original game sound cues, then apply it to audio clips, matching, sequencing and sound-design choices, with text descriptions for every sound.

sections.title: Practice signals
sections.description: Learn what each original cue means.

sections.title: Apply the legend
sections.description: Use the taught meanings in game situations.

questions.prompt: Play the cue. Under the legend, what does this sound signal?
questions.context: Legend: rising three-note chime = ability charged; falling two-note drop = health lost; three quick equal pulses = hazard ahead; one long low tone = action blocked; two high pings = item collected.
questions.explanation: Three notes, each higher than the last, match the legend's rising three-note chime, which this game assigns to ability charged.
questions.transcript: Three smooth notes at 400, 600 and 800 Hz, each higher than the last, starting 0.3 seconds apart.

questions.prompt: Play this second cue. Which legend meaning does the pulse pattern match?
questions.context: Legend: rising three-note chime = ability charged; falling two-note drop = health lost; three quick equal pulses = hazard ahead; one long low tone = action blocked; two high pings = item collected.
questions.explanation: Three short pulses at the same pitch match the legend's three quick equal pulses, which this game assigns to hazard ahead.
questions.transcript: Three very short beeps, all at 500 Hz, starting 0.2 seconds apart.

questions.prompt: Match each game event to the cue the legend assigns to it.
questions.context: Legend: falling two-note drop = health lost; one long low tone = action blocked; two high pings = item collected. Pickups of any kind use the item cue.
questions.explanation: Coins and keys are both pickups, so they share the two-ping cue. The locked door is a blocked action, and the fall costs health.

questions.prompt: A player holds the attack button and the meter fills. Which cue fits this moment under the legend?
questions.context: Legend: rising three-note chime = ability charged; falling two-note drop = health lost; three quick equal pulses = hazard ahead; one long low tone = action blocked; two high pings = item collected.
questions.explanation: A filled meter means an ability is ready, which the legend marks with the rising three-note chime. The other cues describe damage, danger, pickups or blocked actions.

questions.prompt: Order the cues in the sequence the player hears them in this story.
questions.context: Story: a warning sounds before a hit lands. After the hit, the player grabs a shield item. Only once the shield is held does its ability begin charging until ready.
questions.explanation: The warning precedes the hit, the hit precedes the pickup, and the pickup precedes the charge. The story chains the four cues into one possible order.

questions.prompt: A player stands in a poison cloud and hears this cue twice. What does each repeat signal?
questions.context: Legend: falling two-note drop = health lost; rising three-note chime = ability charged; two high pings = item collected; one long low tone = action blocked. Each cloud tick removes some health.
questions.explanation: The cue is the falling two-note drop, which means health lost. Hearing it once per cloud tick tells the player damage is repeating while they stay put.
questions.transcript: Two repeats of a falling pair: a 700 Hz note followed by a 400 Hz note, with a pause between repeats.

questions.prompt: Choose the cue design for each situation that follows the stated sound-design rules.
questions.context: Rules: frequent minor events get short, simple cues. Rare major events get longer, richer cues. Blocked actions use low pitch, not bright rising pitch.
questions.explanation: Short cues keep common events from becoming annoying, longer fanfares make rare moments feel special, and low pitch separates failure from success.

cells.label: Coin pickup that happens 50 times per level
Defeating the final boss, once per game
Trying to fire an empty weapon

questions.prompt: Which addition gives the hazard-ahead warning to a player who cannot hear the pulses?
questions.context: The hazard cue is three quick equal pulses. The game wants the same information available without relying on sound.
questions.explanation: A caption with a directional icon carries the warning visually. Louder, more, or longer pulses are still sound, so they do not help a player who cannot hear them.

options.label: Show an on-screen icon and caption saying hazard ahead

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All sounds are original synthesized tones with text descriptions. Cue meanings are taught by the legend in each question, not universal rules. Scores are out of 8.

title: The Last Move Mystery
description: Work together on one shared device to rewind a tiny eight-square token game, picking legal previous moves and ordering short move chains from the finish back to the start.

sections.title: Single-move rewinds
sections.description: Undo one move at a time.

sections.title: Reverse chains
sections.description: Rebuild the last three moves.

sections.title: Rewind table
sections.description: Fill in the shared solved card.

questions.prompt: The token finished on square 5 after a Hop card. Which square did it start from?
questions.context: Invented mini-game: eight squares, 1 to 8, in a clockwise circle (after 8 comes 1). Cards: Step moves 1 clockwise, Hop moves 2 clockwise, Leap moves 3 clockwise, Back moves 1 counterclockwise.
questions.explanation: A Hop adds 2 squares clockwise, so the token must have started two squares before 5, which is square 3.

questions.prompt: The token finished on square 2 after a Leap card. Which square did it start from?
questions.context: Same mini-game: squares 1 to 8 in a clockwise circle, and 8 is followed by 1. Leap moves 3 squares clockwise.
questions.explanation: Counting a Leap forward from square 7 goes 8, 1, 2, wrapping past the end of the board. No other listed square lands on 2.

questions.prompt: The token started on square 6 and finished on square 1. Which card was played?
questions.context: Same mini-game: squares 1 to 8 clockwise with wraparound. Step is +1, Hop is +2, Leap is +3 clockwise, and Back is 1 counterclockwise.
questions.explanation: From 6 the clockwise path runs 7, 8, 1, which is three squares. Step reaches 7, Hop reaches 8, and Back reaches 5.

questions.prompt: The token finished on square 4 after a clockwise card. Which start square and card were legal?
questions.context: Same mini-game with clockwise cards Step +1, Hop +2, Leap +3. Extra rule: a Leap may only be played from an even-numbered square. Back is not a clockwise card.
questions.explanation: Square 2 plus a Hop lands on 4. Square 1 with a Leap also lands on 4 but is illegal because 1 is odd. Back is not clockwise, and 3 plus a Hop reaches 5.

questions.prompt: The token finished on square 8. Order these recorded moves from the last move back to the earliest.
questions.context: Same mini-game. Each move began on the square where the previous move ended. The even-square Leap rule from the earlier puzzle does not apply here. Use the move arrows to put the final move at the top and the earliest move at the bottom.
questions.explanation: The chain is 2 to 4, then 4 to 5, then 5 to 8. Reading it backward, the Leap ending on 8 comes first, then the Step, then the Hop.

questions.prompt: The token finished on square 3. Order these moves from the last move back to the earliest.
questions.context: Same mini-game, with wraparound. Each move began on the square where the previous move ended. Put the final move at the top and the earliest at the bottom.
questions.explanation: The forward chain is 7 to 6 with Back, 6 to 1 with a wrapping Leap, then 1 to 3 with Hop. Reversed, the Hop comes first, then the Leap, then the Back.

questions.prompt: Fill in the rewind table: for each finish and card, choose the square where the token started.
questions.context: Same mini-game: squares 1 to 8 clockwise with wraparound. Step +1, Hop +2, Leap +3 clockwise, and Back 1 counterclockwise.
questions.explanation: Undo each card: a Step finishing on 1 began on 8, a Back finishing on 2 began on 3, and a Hop finishing on 7 began on 5.

questions.prompt: The token finished on square 6. Connect each card to the start square that could produce that finish.
questions.context: Same mini-game with all four cards: Step +1, Hop +2, Leap +3 clockwise, Back 1 counterclockwise. Connect every card to every start square that works. No other extra rules apply.
questions.explanation: Step comes from 5, Hop from 4, Leap from 3, and Back from 7. Square 8 reaches 1, 2, 3 or 7, never 6, so it stays unconnected.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: The board, cards and rules are an invented mini-game, with every rule stated in each puzzle. Gather around one device and solve together, and talk through each rewind before locking in an answer.

title: Pumpkin Patch Mini-Golf
description: Apply the original Pumpkin Patch Mini-Golf rulebook: stroke counts, penalties for illegal obstacle contact, legal constraints, scoring, and turn ordering by lowest score. Pure rule application on the invented rules; no physical instructions.

questions.prompt: A player takes 3 strokes but contacts a pumpkin obstacle illegally. Penalty is +2. What is the hole score?
questions.context: Original rules: hole score = strokes + penalties. Illegal pumpkin contact = +2 penalty. Legal path only around marked zones.
questions.explanation: 3 strokes + 2 penalty = 5.

questions.prompt: Order the scoring calculation steps.
questions.context: Count strokes, add any penalties for illegal contacts, compare to par if needed, record total.
questions.explanation: Strokes, check illegal, add penalty, record.

questions.prompt: Compute final scores for each player situation.
questions.context: Strokes + penalties.

questions.prompt: Par is 3. Player scores 5 with one penalty. Relative to par?
questions.context: Over par by score - par.

questions.prompt: Match each action to its most specific outcome under the original toy rulebook (completed hole versus still in progress).
questions.context: Original fictional Pumpkin Patch Mini-Golf rulebook only: illegal contact (pumpkin touch or out-of-bounds marker) adds +2 penalty. Legal movement that stays in the marked path but has not yet completed the hole is still in progress (no final score yet). A hole completed in exactly 2 legal strokes with no contact receives final score 2. One-to-many mapping is unique by most-specific category. Turn order remains lowest current total score first.

left.label: Stays in marked path (still in progress, hole not completed)
Hole completed in 2 legal strokes, no contact

right.label: Legal movement still in progress (no final score yet)

questions.explanation: Illegal contact (pumpkin or out-of-bounds) maps to the +2 penalty target (reused). Marked-path movement that has not finished the hole maps to the still-in-progress target (no final score). Completing the hole in 2 clean strokes maps to the completed-hole final-score-2 target. Most-specific exclusive categories.

questions.prompt: Three players have totals 12, 15, 10. Who plays first next hole?
questions.context: Original: lowest total score plays first (ascending order).
questions.explanation: Lowest score 10 plays first.

questions.prompt: Order players by turn sequence for next hole given scores 8, 11, 9, 7.
questions.context: Ascending score order: lowest first.
questions.explanation: 7 then 8 then 9 then 11.

questions.prompt: Match each case to its most specific applicable rule-card outcome under the original toy rulebook.
questions.context: Original fictional rule cards (fiction only, not real mini-golf): (1) illegal contact adds +2 to the score; (2) a clean completed hole has final score equal to the strokes taken; (3) an out-of-turn attempt must wait and, once corrected, incurs no additional penalty; (4) within-bounds movement that is still in progress incurs no boundary penalty but does not yet produce a final hole score. Choose the most specific named card.

left.label: Within-bounds movement still in progress case

right.label: Clean completed hole: final score = strokes
Out-of-turn: wait, no additional penalty once corrected
Within-bounds still in progress: no boundary penalty, no final hole score yet

questions.explanation: Each left case maps to its uniquely named rule card: illegal contact adds +2; a clean completed hole scores exactly the strokes taken; an out-of-turn attempt waits with no extra penalty after correction; within-bounds movement that has not finished the hole has no boundary penalty and no final score yet. Most-specific exclusive outcomes.

sources.label: Original fictional Pumpkin Patch Mini-Golf rulebook for strokes, penalties, constraints and ordering

note: Original toy rulebook only. No physical instructions or real game advice. Graphs list every valid link; matches reuse targets only when semantically identical by rule.

title: The Night Archive: Save the Last Atlas
description: Read a ghostly patrol, preserve an escape route and choose when a diversion must become a defence. Eight supplied tabletop checkpoints lead to a protected atlas and the opening of the dawn shutters.

questions.prompt: How do you guarantee the courier takes the unguarded entrance to the archive?
questions.context: Original tabletop encounter. Supplied checkpoint: Goal: carry the atlas to the exit before the Warden erases it. Start safely outside. The Warden has committed to either the Gallery or the Reading Room, but its card is face down. Each room has its own entrance from outside and its own onward door to the Vault. You may make one preparation and then choose an entrance. READ reveals the committed room. LURE sends the Warden to a named room, but only if that room was not already its destination; otherwise it switches to the other room. WEDGE holds a door open but does not affect the Warden. You cannot enter the occupied room.
questions.explanation: READ gives the information needed to choose the unguarded room in either case. The LURE gamble can backfire: if Gallery was already the destination, the Warden switches to Reading Room. A held door does not make an occupied room safe.

options.label: Use LURE on Gallery, then enter Reading Room.
Use WEDGE on the Gallery door, then enter Gallery.
Use READ, then enter whichever room the Warden did not choose.

questions.prompt: Where should the single WEDGE go so both couriers can still reach the exit after the shutters fall?
questions.context: Original tabletop encounter. Supplied checkpoint: READ revealed Gallery; the atlas courier entered Reading Room safely. A second courier now stands in Gallery after the Warden has moved on. Board links: Reading Room—Vault, Gallery—Vault, Vault—Exit. All three doorways will close; each courier can cross their doorway into the Vault before that happens, but neither can cross a second doorway in time. A WEDGE preserves exactly one doorway through the closure. The Warden is away for this checkpoint.
questions.explanation: Both couriers can enter the Vault before closure. Their remaining shared route is Vault—Exit, so that is the bottleneck to preserve. Wedging either entrance leaves both couriers on the wrong side of the closed exit door.

questions.prompt: Place a LURE where it protects the atlas without drawing the Warden onto the handoff.
questions.context: Original tabletop encounter. Supplied checkpoint: Both couriers are now in the Vault; the atlas waits there. Vault—Exit is wedged open. For this turn the public Warden card says SEARCH VAULT. LURE replaces that destination with one named empty room, provided it differs from the printed destination. The courier will carry the atlas from Vault into Exit after placing the lure. Gallery and Reading Room are empty; Reading Room is sealed and cannot receive a lure. Exit is empty now but will hold the courier when the Warden arrives.
questions.explanation: Gallery is empty, reachable by the lure and off the handoff route. Exit is a trap despite being empty at placement: the courier will be there when the Warden responds. Vault is neither empty nor different from the printed destination.

questions.prompt: Order this recovery so the Warden follows the diversion before the atlas moves.
questions.context: Original tabletop encounter. Supplied checkpoint: The atlas is still in Vault for this supplied replay. A LURE token is in Gallery. The Warden stands in the Vault doorway. Ringing the gallery bell activates the lure and immediately moves the Warden to Gallery. Taking the atlas while the Warden is at the doorway loses the atlas. Carrying the atlas out requires first taking it. Close the atlas cover only after it is in Exit; closing it anywhere else seals the map before it can be carried.
questions.explanation: Activate the bell to clear the doorway, take the atlas, carry it through the preserved exit route, then close its cover. Taking it before the diversion loses it; closing early makes it immovable. The order solves the encounter through consequences rather than a generic list of card priorities.

items.label: Close the atlas cover in Exit.

questions.prompt: Assign the three remaining cards so neither courier nor their route is lost.
questions.context: Original tabletop encounter. Supplied checkpoint: The first atlas crossing is complete, but its protective case is still inside. Courier Ana is in Gallery; courier Bo is in Reading Room. Both must next reach Vault and then Exit with the case. Forecasts: the Warden will visit Gallery before Ana can leave; Reading Room’s exit will close before Bo can leave; the Warden will then choose a route from a face-down card while both wait safely in Vault. VEIL protects one courier against one visit. WEDGE preserves one doorway. READ reveals a face-down route so they can choose the safe final crossing. One card of each kind remains; assign each once.
questions.explanation: Ana needs VEIL against the announced visit. Bo needs WEDGE for the closing doorway. The hidden final route needs READ; neither protection nor a door wedge reveals it. This distributes scarce, different resources across three threats instead of spending everything on the most visible one.

left.label: Prepare the final crossing from Vault

questions.prompt: The Warden has learned the diversion. Which revised plan protects the carrier?
questions.context: Original tabletop encounter. Supplied checkpoint: The case carrier is in Vault. This checkpoint supplies a fresh VEIL and a LURE. The revealed Warden card is INSPECT: ignore all lures and visit the carrier’s current room before anyone may move. A VEIL protects its holder for that visit and is then discarded. The door to Exit is already open. You may play one card before the inspection, then move after it.
questions.explanation: INSPECT counters the lure and happens before movement. VEIL absorbs that visit, leaving the carrier able to use the open exit afterwards. The key is responding to the revealed counterplay rather than repeating the previous winning diversion.

options.label: Lure the Warden back to Gallery, then move.
Veil the carrier, let the inspection pass, then move.
Hold both cards and move before the inspection.

questions.prompt: Do you take the tempting detour or secure the atlas? Choose the only guaranteed win.
questions.context: Original tabletop encounter. Supplied checkpoint: The case and atlas are together in Exit. You have one last move before the final erasure. A side alcove contains an optional illustration; entering it uses that move, even with VEIL. Placing the atlas in its case on the exit lectern also uses that move and protects it permanently. The win condition is the protected atlas. The illustration is a bonus only if the atlas is protected first. There is no further scoring move before the erasure.
questions.explanation: The case on the lectern is the only permanent protection available before erasure. VEIL protects a courier against a visit, not an unprotected atlas against the final erasure. A bonus cannot compensate for losing the stated objective.

options.label: Take the illustration with VEIL, leaving the atlas on the floor.
Place the atlas in its case on the exit lectern.
Leave the illustration, keep the atlas in hand and wait.

questions.prompt: The atlas survives. Which final arrangement opens the shutters and ends the Warden’s patrol?
questions.context: Original tabletop encounter. Supplied checkpoint: After the scoring round, resetting the exit door is a free cleanup action, not another scoring move. Final board: the protected atlas is on the exit lectern; both couriers stand in Exit; the Warden remains inside. The dawn mechanism opens when the exit door is closed and the atlas remains on the lectern. A WEDGE still holds the exit door open. Removing it lets the door close automatically. Taking the atlas off the lectern stops the dawn mechanism; moving a courier inside traps them when the door closes. Your goal is dawn with both couriers outside the archive.
questions.explanation: The last useful resource has become the last obstruction: the wedge saved the crossing, but now keeps the dawn mechanism from working. Removing it from the safe side closes the door while both couriers stay in Exit. The shutters open, the Warden’s patrol ends, and the atlas’s map of the archive is preserved.

options.label: Carry the atlas off the lectern and remove the wedge.
Send a courier inside to remove the wedge, then close the door.
Remove the wedge from the Exit side and leave the atlas on the lectern.

sources.label: Original Night Archive tabletop rules, public states and encounter

note: An original, non-graphic tabletop encounter for solo play or discussion in one shared attempt. Each question supplies its own checkpoint, hand and forecast; earlier answers do not change later states. No live opponent, hidden actual player information, money or turn-by-turn multiplayer system is involved.
